result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.algebraic_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the algebraic connectivity of an undirected graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L58945-L59006){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.algebraic_connectivity( normalized=False, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Algebraic connectivity](/assets/graphs/algebraic-connectivity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left, a six-node cycle whose closing edge F–A is in the accent color; right, the same nodes without that edge (dashed), a path. The cycle's algebraic connectivity is 1.0 and the path's only 0.268: the path is much easier to cut in two." width="100%"} The algebraic connectivity (Fiedler, 1973) is the second smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian. It is `0` exactly when the graph is disconnected, and grows the harder the graph is to cut apart: it bounds the edge and node connectivity from below, and controls how fast random walks mix, synchronization spreads, and consensus is reached. Bottleneck graphs (two clusters joined by a thin link, long paths) have small values; expanders and dense graphs have large ones. The matching eigenvector is `fiedler_vector()`. Large graphs use a sparse eigensolver, so this scales to big networks. Matches NetworkX's `algebraic_connectivity()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, use the normalized Laplacian (see `normalized_laplacian_matrix()`). Default is `False`. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph. Weights must be non-negative. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The algebraic connectivity (`0.0` for a disconnected graph). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, has fewer than two nodes, or has a negative weight. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle is better connected than a path with the same nodes, and a complete graph best of all: ::: {#4cf26811 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ( round(ec.Graph().add_path_graph(6).algebraic_connectivity(), 3), round(ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6).algebraic_connectivity(), 3), round(ec.Graph().add_full_graph(6).algebraic_connectivity(), 3), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.268, 1.0, 6.0) ``` ::: :::
